en: 1. Introduction Chapter. The *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra*, Chapter One: The Introduction.
Translated during the Northern Liang Dynasty by an unknown translator.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the great city of Rājagṛha.
He was accompanied by a great assembly of ten thousand bhikṣus, all of whom had attained the path of arhatship; their names were Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, and other such arhats.
Furthermore, there were two thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas together with him, their names being Vimukta Bodhisattva, Cittarāja Bodhisattva, Aniketastha Bodhisattva, and other such bodhisattvas.
Additionally, there were eighty thousand elders together with him, their names being Brahmacarin Elder, Mahābrahmacarin Elder, Jyotiṣka Elder, and other such elders.
Furthermore, there were six hundred trillion devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others.

At that time, the Venerable One was surrounded by a great assembly, and for the sake of the multitude he preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Beneficial Practice of Original Enlightenment, the Ultimate Reality, Certainty, Non-arising, Signlessness, and Single Flavor*.

If one hears this sutra, or even receives and upholds a single four-line verse, that person shall enter the ground of the Buddha’s wisdom; they will be able to teach and transform sentient beings through skillful means, acting as a great spiritual friend to all sentient beings.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, he sat cross-legged and immediately entered the Vajra Samādhi, his body and mind unmoving.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu in the assembly named Āgada, who rose from his seat, joined his palms, knelt on his right knee, and wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"O Honored One, whose great compassion is fulfilled, Whose wisdom penetrates all without obstruction,..."
In order to extensively deliver all sentient beings, he teaches the meaning of the Single Truth.
All are brought through the flavor of the One Way; he never employs the Lesser Vehicle.
Regarding the essence of the meaning thus taught, it is entirely free from what is unreal.
Entering the various stages of the Buddha’s wisdom, they are firmly established in the limit of reality;
all who hear this transcend the world, and there are none who do not attain liberation.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas all bring sentient beings across to the other shore.
For the sake of the assembly, he asks extensively and profoundly, knowing the mark of the dharma’s quiescence.
Having entered the state of certainty, through the Tathāgata’s wisdom and skillful means, he shall preach for the entry into reality; all that accords with it is the One Vehicle.
There are no diverse flavors; just as a single rain moistens all,
causing every blade of grass to flourish, each according to its own nature,
so too does the moisture of the single flavor of the Dharma universally suffuse all things.
Just as that single rain moistens all, causing the sprouts of bodhi to grow;
entering the adamantine flavor and realizing the samādhi of the reality of the Dharma,
one decisively cuts off doubt and regret, accomplishing the seal of the One Dharma.
**Chapter Two: On the Dharma of Signlessness** *The Vajrasamādhi Sūtra, Chapter Two: On the Dharma of Signlessness* At that time, the Venerable One arose from samādhi and spoke these words:
“The ground of wisdom of all Buddhas enters into the true mark of dharmas because of its definitive nature; thus, skillful means and supernormal powers are all beneficially signless.”

The single awakened ultimate meaning is difficult to understand and difficult to enter; it is not within the scope of knowledge or vision of the followers of the two vehicles, but can only be known by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. To deliver sentient beings, they preach a single flavor.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Liberation rose from his seat, joined his palms, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable One!

If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma has departed from the world and only the Semblance Dharma remains, during the final kalpa, sentient beings amidst the five turbidities will commit many evil karmas and cycle through the three realms of existence without any prospect of escape."

"I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will proclaim for the sake of sentient beings in future generations the single flavor, the definitive truth, so that those beings may likewise attain liberation.
The Buddha said, "Good son!

That you are able to question me regarding the causes for transcending the world, desiring to transform sentient beings so that they may attain the fruit of transcendence—this is a great matter, inconceivable.
Because of my great kindness and great compassion, if I were not to speak, I would fall into stinginess and greed.
"You all, listen attentively and listen attentively; I shall proclaim it for you. Good sons!
If one transforms sentient beings such that there is no birth in transformation, nor the non-arising of non-transformation, that transformation is truly great."

I cause those sentient beings to all be free from the self of the mind; the self of the mind is fundamentally empty and quiescent. If one attains the emptiness of the mind, the mind will not undergo illusory transformation.
Without illusion and without transformation, one attains non-arising; the non-arising mind abides in non-transformation.
The Bodhisattva Liberation addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The nature of the minds of sentient beings is fundamentally empty and quiescent; the essence of this empty and quiescent mind has no form or characteristics."
"How should one cultivate the practice to attain the mind of original emptiness?
I pray that the Buddha, out of his great compassion, will expound this for me.
The Buddha said:

“Bodhisattva! All mental characteristics are fundamentally without origin; being fundamentally without an origin, they are empty, quiescent, and unarisen. If the mind is unarisen, one enters into emptiness and quiescence; with the ground of the mind being empty and quiescent, one attains the emptiness of the mind.”
“Good son! The mind of signlessness is without mind and without self; the characteristics of all dharmas are likewise so.
The Bodhisattva Liberation addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Venerable One!
If all sentient beings possess a self or possess a mind, by what dharma can they be awakened so that those beings may emerge from these bonds?”
The Buddha said,
"Good son! If there is a self, have them contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination."
The twelve links of dependent origination fundamentally arise from cause and effect; that which is produced by cause and effect originates in mental activity.
Since even the mind does not exist, how much less can there be a body?
If there were a self, one would cause the view of existence to be extinguished.
If there is no self, cause the view of non-existence to cease.
If the mind arises, cause the nature of cessation to cease;
if the mind ceases, cause the nature of arising to cease.
To extinguish this nature of views is to enter the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Why is this? That which is originally born does not perish; that which is originally extinguished is not born. What does not perish is not born; what is not born does not perish. All dharmas are likewise so.
The Bodhisattva Vimukti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable One!
If there are sentient beings who perceive the arising of dharmas, what kind of views should one cause them to extinguish?"
"When one perceives the cessation of dharmas, what views does one cause to cease?
The Buddha said, "Bodhisattva!"
If there are sentient beings who, when seeing phenomena arise, cause them to eliminate the view of non-existence;
and when seeing phenomena cease, cause them to eliminate the view of existence.
If they eliminate these views, they will realize the true non-existence of phenomena, entering the state of certainty and the certainty of non-arising.
The Bodhisattva Liberation addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Causing those sentient beings to abide in non-arising is itself non-arising."
The Buddha said:
"To abide in non-arising is itself arising. Why is this so?"
Non-abiding and non-arising—this is indeed non-arising.
O Bodhisattva!
If one gives rise to non-arising, one uses arising to extinguish arising; when both arising and extinction are extinguished, original arising is non-arising.
"The mind is eternally empty and tranquil; the nature of emptiness has no abiding place. That the mind has no abiding place is precisely non-arising.
The Bodhisattva Liberation addressed the Buddha, saying, "Venerable One!"
If the mind has no abiding, what is there to cultivate or study?
Is it for those in training (śaikṣa),
or is it for those beyond training (aśaikṣa)?
The Buddha said: “Bodhisattva!
The mind of non-arising has no entering or exiting; it is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, quiescent and unmoving, neither a learner (śaikṣa) nor one beyond learning (aśaikṣa).”
"There is neither one in training nor one beyond training; this is what it means to be beyond training.
It is not that there is no one in training that constitutes 'that which is learned.
Liberation Bodhisattva then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Venerable One!
How is it that the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is quiescent and immovable?
The Buddha said:

“The Tathāgatagarbha is such that its nature is obscured by the characteristics of arising, ceasing, and discursive cognition, so that its principle is not manifest; yet the nature of this Tathāgatagarbha is quiescent and immovable.
The Bodhisattva Vimukta addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! [The Tathāgatagarbha]...”
"What is the characteristic of discerning cognition regarding arising and ceasing? The Buddha said, "Bodhisattva!"
In principle, there can be no "yes" or "no.
If there were such "yes" or "no," it would give rise to various thoughts and myriad deliberations; these are the marks of arising and ceasing.
O Bodhisattva!

When one contemplates the principle of the fundamental nature and characteristics, it is inherently complete; a thousand thoughts and ten thousand deliberations do not benefit this principle, but merely cause agitation and confusion, causing one to lose the sovereign king of the original mind.
If there is no thought or deliberation, then there is neither arising nor ceasing.

When things do not arise according to reality, the various consciousnesses become tranquil and still; as their continuous flow ceases to arise, one attains the purity of the five dharmas—this is called the Mahāyāna.
Bodhisattva!
Upon entering the purity of the five dharmas, the mind is immediately free from delusion.
If there is no delusion, one enters the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realized noble wisdom;
those who enter this stage of wisdom thoroughly know that all things are fundamentally unborn;
knowing they are fundamentally unborn, one is free from false conceptualization.
The Bodhisattva Vimukti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable One! For one who is free from conceptual construction, there should be no cessation."
The Buddha said:
"Bodhisattva! Delusion is fundamentally unarisen; there is no delusion that can be extinguished."
Knowing that the mind is no-mind, there is no mind to be stilled.
Without division and without distinction, the manifesting consciousness does not arise; since there is no arising to be stilled, this is neither "stilling" nor "not-stilling."
"Why is this? Because cessation itself has no cessation.
The Bodhisattva Liberation addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Venerable One!
If cessation is itself non-cessation, then cessation is precisely arising; what, then, is meant by ‘non-arising’?
The Buddha said:

“Bodhisattva! You should bring this arising to rest; once it has been brought to rest, there is no further resting. One neither dwells in non-resting nor dwells in non-dwelling. What, then, is this arising?”
The Bodhisattva Liberation addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable One!
In the mind of non-arising, what is there to be grasped or abandoned?"
"In what kind of dharmic characteristics does he abide? The Buddha said:
"In a mind of non-arising, which neither grasps nor rejects."
"One dwells in non-mind and dwells in non-dharmas.
The Bodhisattva Vimukta addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Venerable One!"
"What is it to dwell in non-mind and to dwell in non-dharma?
The Buddha said:
"Not giving rise to the mind is dwelling in non-mind."
Non-arising in phenomena is abiding in non-dharmas.
Son of good family!
The non-arising of mental phenomena is itself without dependence.
Not dwelling in any conditioned activities, the mind is ever empty and tranquil, devoid of any marks of differentiation.

It is like space, which has neither movement nor stillness; it is without arising, without action, without "that," and without "this. One attains the eye of the empty mind and the body of the empty Dharma; the five aggregates and six sense bases are all entirely empty and tranquil.
Good son! One who cultivates the dharma of emptiness does not rely on the triple world and does not dwell upon the marks of precepts;
they are pure and without thought, neither grasping nor relinquishing.
“Nature is equal to the vajra, indestructible as the Triple Gem;
the empty mind is unmoving, fully possessing the six pāramitās.
Liberation Bodhisattva then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable One! These six pāramitās all possess marks.
Can a dharma that possesses marks transcend the world?"
The Buddha said:
"Good son! The six pāramitās that I have taught are signless and unconditioned."

Why is this? If a person is free from desire, their mind is constantly pure; through truthful speech and skillful means, they benefit others with fundamental benefit—this is the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
To have firm resolve and mindfulness, with a mind that is always non-abiding, pure and undefiled, and unattached to the three realms—this is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).

To cultivate emptiness and sever the fetters, not relying on any forms of existence, keeping the three karmas tranquil, and not dwelling in body or mind—this is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

To remain far removed from names and numbers, to sever the views of emptiness and existence, and to penetrate deeply into the emptiness of the aggregates (skandhas)—this is the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).

To be simultaneously detached from both emptiness and quiescence, not to dwell in any forms of emptiness, for the mind to abide in non-abiding, and not to dwell even in the great emptiness—this is the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā).
The mind has no characteristic of mind; it does not grasp at empty space, all conditioned phenomena do not arise, and it does not realize cessation.

The mind has no entering or exiting; its nature is eternally equal. The reality-limit of all dharmas is of a definitive nature; it does not rely on the stages and does not dwell in wisdom—this is the *prajñāpāramitā*.
“Good son! These six pāramitās all attain their fundamental benefit, enter the nature of certainty, transcendently emerge from the world, and achieve unimpeded liberation.”
Good son! Such characteristics of the dharma of liberation are all practices of signlessness; they are neither understanding nor non-understanding—this is called liberation. Why is this?

"The characteristics of liberation are signless, without activity, without movement, and without agitation; they are the tranquility of nirvana, yet one does not even grasp at the characteristic of nirvana.
Upon hearing these words, the Bodhisattva Liberation was greatly delighted and experienced what he had never known before. Desiring to proclaim the meaning of this principle, he spoke in verse:
"The Greatly Awakened One, the Perfected Honored One, Expounds the Dharma for the sake of the multitudes."
All are taught within the Single Vehicle; there are no paths of two vehicles.
This single flavor and signless benefit is like the great void, which has nothing it does not accommodate, yet according to their natures, each is distinct.
All attain their original state, just as that which is free from mind and self is accomplished through a single dharma; all various modes of existence, whether identical or different,
fully obtain their fundamental benefit, extinguishing the dualistic views of subject and object.
In the tranquility of nirvāṇa, one does not abide even in the realization of attainment.
Entering the state of certainty, it is signless and without activity;
it is the ground of the empty mind’s cessation, where the tranquil mind is unborn.
Possessing that same vajra-nature, they do not destroy the Three Jewels;
endowed with the six pāramitās, they deliver all sentient beings.
Transcending the three realms, they do so entirely without recourse to the Hīnayāna.
"The Dharma-seal of the single flavor is that which is accomplished by the One Vehicle.

At that time, the great assembly, having heard this teaching, felt immense joy in their hearts; they attained liberation from the self of the mind, entered into emptiness and signlessness, became vast and expansive, and all achieved certainty, severing their fetters and exhausting their outflows.

Chapter Three: On Non-arising Practice The Vajrasamādhi Sūtra, Chapter Three: On Non-arising Practice At that time, Bodhisattva Cittarāja, having heard the Buddha’s teaching on how that which transcends the three realms is inconceivable, rose from his seat, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha in verse:
“The meaning spoken by the Tathāgata Transcends the world and is without marks.”
Can all sentient beings attain the exhaustion of outflows?
By severing fetters and emptying the mind of self, there is then no further birth.
How is it that by having no further birth, one attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mind-King Bodhisattva, saying:

“Good son! The dharma of the patience regarding non-arising is fundamentally without arising. All conditioned phenomena are non-arising, yet they are not the practice of non-arising; to claim one has attained the patience of non-arising is itself a delusion.”
Cittarāja Bodhisattva said:
“Venerable One!
Is the attainment of the patience of non-arising itself a delusion?”
"Then non-attainment and non-endurance would not be false! The Buddha said, "No."
Why is this? To have no attainment and no patience is itself attainment; to have attainment and patience is itself birth.
Birth arises from attainment, and all dharmas that are attained are collectively false and illusory.
Cittarāja Bodhisattva said:
“Venerable One!
How is it that a mind which is neither patient nor arising is not false?”
The Buddha said:
"That which is neither patient nor a mind of arising has no form or substance; it is like the nature of fire, which, though residing within wood, exists nowhere because its nature is determinate."

There are only names and only words; their intrinsic nature cannot be apprehended. To explain their underlying principle, one provisionally designates them as "names," yet even these names cannot be apprehended.
The characteristics of the mind are likewise: no location for them can be seen. To know the mind in this way is to have no arising of the mind.

“Good son! The nature and characteristics of this mind are like the āmalaka fruit: fundamentally, it is not self-arisen, nor does it arise from another, nor do they arise together, nor does it arise through causes, nor is it non-arising.”
Why is this? Because conditions undergo succession.
Conditioned arising is not birth; the cessation of conditions is not extinction. Hiddenness and manifestation are without marks; their fundamental principle is quiescent extinction.
In the state of non-existence, no abiding place is perceived, because of its definitive nature.

This definitive nature is neither one nor different, neither annihilated nor eternal, neither entering nor emerging, neither arising nor ceasing; it is free from all four types of false attribution and transcends the path of verbal expression.
The mind-nature, which is unborn, is likewise so.
What is meant by speaking of birth and non-birth, or of having patience and lacking patience?
If one speaks of the mind as having attainment, abiding, or views, then such a person has not attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Prajñāpāramitā is that which, throughout the long night, discerns the nature of the mind; it knows the nature of the mind to be thus:
its nature is likewise such—unborn and without activity.
Thus spoke Bodhisattva Mind-King.
"Venerable One! If the mind is fundamentally such that it does not arise within formations (*saṃskāra*), then all formations are non-arising.
When arising formations do not arise, and non-arising is without formations, this is precisely the non-arising of formations."
The Buddha said,
"Good son, do you realize the practice of non-arising by means of non-arising?"
Cittarāja Bodhisattva said: “No. Why is this? Because...”

As with the practice of non-arising, its nature and characteristics are empty and quiescent; there is no seeing and no hearing, no gaining and no losing, no speech and no discourse, no knowing and no marks, and no grasping and no relinquishing. How, then, could one take up and realize it?
"If one grasps at realization, that constitutes contentious debate.
To be without contention and without debate is the practice of non-arising.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
“You shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Citta-rāja Bodhisattva said,
“O Venerable One!”
I have not attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?

Within the nature of *bodhi*, there is neither attainment nor loss; there is no awakening and no cognition; there are no marks of discrimination, and within non-discrimination lies the very nature of purity.
The nature is without interval or admixture and is beyond verbal expression; it is neither existent nor non-existent, neither known nor unknown;
all dharmas and practices are likewise so.
Why is this? Because all dharmas and their activities have no fixed location, as they are of a determinate nature.
Fundamentally, there is neither attainment nor non-attainment; how, then, could one attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
The Buddha said: “So it is, so it is.
As you have said, all mental activities do not transcend the signless, quiescent, and unborn essence; the existence of the various consciousnesses is likewise thus.”

Why is this? The eye and visual contact are both entirely empty and quiescent; consciousness is also empty and quiescent, possessing neither the mark of movement nor the mark of non-movement. Within, there are no three feelings (*trivedanā*), for the three feelings are extinguished.

It is likewise with the ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, mental consciousness, as well as the *manas* and *ālayavijñāna*; all of these likewise do not give rise to a mind of extinction or a mind of non-arising.
Whether one gives rise to a mind of quiescent extinction or a mind of non-arising, these are practices of arising, not practices of non-arising.
When a bodhisattva internally gives rise to the three feelings, the three activities, and the three precepts, if they have already been extinguished, the mind arises but does not arise.

The mind is eternally quiescent, without merit and without function; it does not realize the mark of quiescence, nor does it abide in non-realization. Being able to dwell in non-abiding, one upholds the signless *dhāraṇī*; thus, there are no three feelings, three activities, or three precepts—all are utterly quiescent, pure, and non-abiding. One neither enters samādhi nor abides in seated meditation; there is no arising and no activity.
Cittarāja Bodhisattva said:
"Dhyāna can restrain movement and settle all illusory distractions.
Why, then, would one not practice dhyāna?"
The Buddha said:
“The dhyāna of a bodhisattva is movement; non-movement and non-dhyāna is the dhyāna of non-arising.
The nature of dhyāna is non-arising, being free from the characteristics of arising dhyāna.”
The nature of dhyāna has no abiding; it is free from the movement of abiding in dhyāna.
If one knows that the nature of dhyāna is devoid of both motion and stillness, one immediately attains non-arising;
this non-arising prajñā likewise does not rely on abiding, and the mind remains unmoving.
"By means of this wisdom, one attains the non-arising Prajñāpāramitā.
Mind-King Bodhisattva said:
"O Venerable One!"

The non-arising *prajñā* abides nowhere and is not separated from anything; the mind has no place of abiding, and there is no place where the mind dwells. Without abiding and without mind, the mind neither arises nor abides.
When the mind abides in this manner, there is neither arising nor abiding.
Venerable One!
That the mind has neither arising nor abiding is inconceivable!
"Within the inconceivable, can it be said whether it is possible or impossible?
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is."
Upon hearing these words, Bodhisattva Mind-King marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and spoke in verse:
"The Honored One of Great Wisdom, fulfilled, Has extensively expounded the Dharma of non-arising.
We hear what we have never heard before; What was not yet spoken is now being spoken."
Just like pure nectar, which appears only once in a great while, it is difficult to encounter and difficult to conceive; likewise, those who hear it are rare.
It is the unsurpassed field of merit, the most supreme and wondrous medicine.
"For the sake of delivering sentient beings, I now proclaim this teaching.
At that time, having heard this discourse within the assembly, all attained the non-arising of non-arising prajñā.

Chapter Four: The Benefits of Innate Awakening (*Mūla-bodhi-anuśaṃsa-parivarta*) from the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra*. At that time, the Bodhisattva Anabhiniveśa, having heard the Buddha’s teaching on the inconceivable single flavor of reality, came from afar to approach the Tathāgata’s seat. With focused mindfulness and attentive hearing, he entered the state of purity, his body and mind unmoving.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Anabhinivāsin, saying:
"From where have you come?
Where are you going now?"
The Bodhisattva Non-Abiding said:
"Venerable One!
I have come from the originless and now arrive at the place of the originless."
The Buddha said, "You originally did not come from anywhere, and now you fundamentally do not go anywhere.
You have attained the inconceivable fundamental benefit; you are a great Bodhisattva Mahāsattva."
He immediately emitted a great light that illuminated a thousand worlds, and spoke these verses:
"How great is the Bodhisattva!
His wisdom is fully perfected."
Constantly employing fundamental benefit to bring profit to sentient beings,
one abides eternally in this fundamental benefit throughout the four modes of deportment, guiding all the multitudes without coming or going.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Anabhiniveśa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
By what transformative benefit do you cause all the mental consciousnesses of sentient beings to enter the amala-vijñāna?"
The Buddha said:
"All Buddhas and Tathāgatas always transform the various consciousnesses by means of a single awakening, causing them to enter the āmala-vijñāna. Why is this?"

The original enlightenment of all sentient beings constantly awakens all beings with a single awakening, causing them all to attain original enlightenment and realize that all emotional consciousnesses are empty, quiescent, and unborn.
"Why is this? Because the determined nature is fundamentally without movement.
The Bodhisattva Non-Abiding said:
“If all eight consciousnesses arise by taking objects as conditions, how can they be unmoving?
The Buddha said:
“All objects are fundamentally empty, and all consciousnesses are fundamentally empty. Since emptiness has no nature of being conditioned, how can there be arising through conditions?”
The Bodhisattva Wuzhu said,
"If all objects are empty, how can there be seeing?
The Buddha said:
"To perceive [them] is itself delusion. Why is this?
All phenomena are without arising and without marks; they have no inherent names from the beginning and are entirely empty and quiescent."
The characteristics of all dharmas are likewise so;
the bodies of all sentient beings are likewise so.
Since even the body does not exist, how could there be seeing?
The Bodhisattva Anabhinivāsin said:
"All objects are empty, all bodies are empty, and all consciousnesses are empty; awakening, too, should be empty.
The Buddha said:
"That which can be once awakened is neither destroyed nor disintegrated, because its nature is determinate; it is neither empty nor non-empty, for there is neither emptiness nor non-emptiness.
Bodhisattva Non-Abiding said: "All objects are likewise:
they do not possess the characteristic of emptiness, nor do they lack the characteristic of emptiness."
The Buddha said: "It is so.
That which is the object of perception is, by its very nature, fundamentally determined; this determined nature of the faculties has no location."
The Bodhisattva Anabhinivista said, “Awakening is likewise; it has no location.
The Buddha said:
"In this way: because awakening has no locus, it is pure; being pure, there is no awakening.
Because phenomena have no locus, they are pure; being pure, there is no form."
The Bodhisattva Anabhinivista said:
"The mind, the eye, and consciousness are likewise thus.
They are inconceivable!"
The Buddha said:
"The mind, the eye, and consciousness are likewise thus.
They are inconceivable!"
Why is this? Form has no location; it is pure and nameless, and does not enter within.
The eye has no location; it is pure and without seeing, and does not go forth without.
The mind has no location; it is pure and without cessation, having no place of origination.
Consciousness has no location; it is pure and without movement, having no distinct objects of perception.
Their nature is entirely empty and quiescent; their nature has no cognition, yet when there is cognition, it constitutes awakening.
Son of good family!
When one realizes that there is no cognition to be known, all consciousnesses enter [into cessation].

Why is this? Because the path of liberation on the adamantine ground of wisdom (*vajrajñānabhūmi*) severs [all bonds], and having severed them, one enters the ground of non-abiding (*apratiṣṭhita-bhūmi*), where there is no entering or exiting.

The mind abides nowhere in the ground of certainty; that ground is pure like clear lapis lazuli, its nature eternally equal like the great earth, its wondrous observation awakening like the light of the sun’s wisdom, and its benefit and fulfillment attaining the source like the great rain of Dharma.
"One who enters this wisdom enters the ground of the Buddha’s wisdom; one who enters the ground of wisdom is such that the various consciousnesses do not arise.
The Bodhisattva Non-Abiding said:

"What the Tathāgata has spoken of as the power of the noble single awakening and the four great vows of the ground of wisdom is precisely the fundamental root of awakening and sharpness possessed by all sentient beings."
"Why is this? Because all sentient beings are, within this very body, originally and fully endowed [with it].
The Buddha said:

"It is so. Why is this? All sentient beings are fundamentally without outflows (*anāsrava*), being the very root of all wholesome benefits; yet now they possess the thorns of desire, which have not yet been subdued."
The Bodhisattva Wuzhu said:
"If there are sentient beings who have not yet attained fundamental benefit and still engage in gathering [karmic seeds],
how can one subdue those who are difficult to subdue?"
The Buddha said:

“Whether in company or walking alone, through discernment and detachment, turning the mind to dwell in the empty cave, subduing that which is difficult to tame, being liberated from the bonds of Māra, sitting serenely in the open air, one attains parinirvāṇa within the aggregate of consciousness.”
The Bodhisattva Anabhinivṛtti said:
"If the mind attains nirvāṇa alone, without companion, and abides eternally in nirvāṇa, it ought to be liberated.
The Buddha said:
"Permanently abiding in nirvana is the bondage of nirvana. Why is this?
Nirvana is the benefit of original enlightenment, and original enlightenment benefits nirvana; the factors of awakening within nirvana are themselves the factors of original enlightenment."
The nature of awakening is not different; nirvana is not different.
Awakening is fundamentally without arising; nirvana is without arising.
Awakening is fundamentally without cessation; nirvana is without cessation.
Because Nirvana is the fundamental source, there is no attaining of Nirvana, nor is there any Nirvana to be attained; how, then, could there be abiding?
Son of Good Family!
One who has awakened does not abide in Nirvana.
Why is this? Awakening is fundamentally without arising, for it is free from the defilements of sentient beings;
awakening is fundamentally without quiescence, for it is free from the movement of nirvana.
Dwelling in such a stage, the mind has no place of abiding and neither enters nor exits; it enters the amala-vijñāna.
The Bodhisattva Non-Abiding said, “The amala-vijñāna is a place of entry; having a place implies there is something attained, and this is the attainment of dharmas.”
The Buddha said: “No. Why is that? Because...”
It is like a lost son who holds a gold coin in his hand but does not know it exists.
Wandering through the ten directions for fifty years, he suffers from poverty and hardship, devoting himself solely to seeking and begging to sustain his life, yet remains unsatisfied.
Seeing that his son was in such a state, his father said to him:
"Why do you not take and use this gold coin?
Whatever you require shall be fully provided according to your wish."
When the son awoke and found the gold coins, his heart was filled with great joy, and he thought, "I have obtained money.
His father said to him,
"Deluded son!"
"Do not rejoice; the gold coins you have obtained were your original property. You did not acquire them anew, so why should you be glad?
"Good son, the *āmalaka* fruit is also like this."
"Originally there was no mark of emergence; now, it is not entering.
Because of past delusion, it was not non-existent; because of present awakening, it is not entering.
Thus spoke Bodhisattva Non-Abiding.
"The father knew that his son was deluded; why did he wait until fifty years had passed, after traveling through the ten directions and undergoing poverty and hardship, before finally speaking?"
The Buddha said:
"One who has practiced for fifty years may still have a single thought stir;
they travel throughout the ten directions, far-fetched and full of conceptual proliferation."
The Bodhisattva Non-Abiding asked:
"How does the mind move in a single thought-moment?
The Buddha said:
"When a single thought-moment moves, the five aggregates arise together; within the arising of these five aggregates, fifty evils are present.
Bodhisattva Non-Abiding said:
"Traveling afar through pervasive conceptualization and roaming throughout the ten directions, when a single thought-moment arises, it possesses fifty evils."
"How can one cause those sentient beings to not give rise to even a single thought?

The Buddha said, "Cause those sentient beings to settle their minds and spirits, abiding on the ground of vajra with tranquil mindfulness free from arising; when the mind is always peaceful and secure, there is no single thought."
The Bodhisattva Non-Abiding said:
"Inconceivable! When the movement of thought does not arise and the mind is peaceful and secure, this is the benefit of original enlightenment."
Benefit is without movement and eternally exists as non-nonexistence; there is no non-nonexistence, yet this non-nonexistence is not without awakening.
To know that awakening is itself without awakening is the fundamental benefit and fundamental awakening. This awakening is pure, undefiled, and unattached; it is immutable and unchanging.
"Because it is definitive, it is inconceivable. The Buddha said, "So it is."
Having heard these words, the Bodhisattva Non-Abiding attained what he had never experienced before and spoke in verse:
“O Honored One, Great Awakened One, You have taught the Dharma of birth through non-thought.
The mind of non-thought and non-birth Is a mind that is eternally born and never extinguished.”
"The benefit of awakening to original enlightenment is to benefit all who possess original enlightenment;
it is like obtaining gold coins—the very thing obtained is itself non-attainment.
At that time, when the great assembly heard these words, they all attained the prajñāpāramitā that benefits original enlightenment.
Chapter Five: Entering the Reality-Limit (*bhūtakoṭi*). In this chapter of the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra*, the Tathāgata spoke these words:
"The bodhisattvas, through their fundamental benefits, have entered deeply; they are able to deliver sentient beings."

If it is later and not the proper time, one should speak of benefit as one speaks of the Dharma at the proper time; one should not speak merely according to what is favorable or unfavorable, nor in terms of identity or difference, but should speak in accordance with reality.

Leading all emotions and cognitions to flow into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), do not allow the multitude to scoop up that empty wind; cause all those beings to partake of the single flavor of divine milk. Whether mundane or supramundane, abiding or non-abiding, they enter and exit the five emptinesses without grasping or rejecting.

Why is this? All phenomena have the characteristic of emptiness; their nature is neither existent nor non-existent, neither non-existent nor not non-existent, neither not non-existent nor not existent. They lack a determinate nature, do not abide in existence or non-existence, and are not that existence or non-existence.
"The wisdom of both ordinary beings and sages can fathom what is hidden; if the various bodhisattvas understand this benefit, they shall immediately attain Bodhi.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Mahāsthāmaprāpta who rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"As the Buddha has taught, there is neither grasping nor abandoning in the entering and exiting of the five emptinesses.
How is it that one does not grasp or abandon these five emptinesses?
The Buddha said:
“Bodhisattva! The five emptinesses are: the three realms of existence are empty;
the shadows of the six destinies are empty; the characteristics of phenomena are empty; the characteristics of names are empty; and the meaning of mind-consciousness is empty.”
Bodhisattva!
Such emptinesses as these do not abide in emptiness; emptiness has no characteristic of emptiness. In a dharma that is without characteristics, what is there to be grasped or abandoned?
Upon entering the stage of non-grasping, one enters the three kinds of emptiness.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta asked,
"What are the three emptinesses?
The Buddha said:
"The three emptinesses are:
the characteristic of emptiness is also empty, the emptiness of emptiness is also empty, and that which is emptied is also empty.
Such emptinesses do not abide in the three characteristics, yet they are not devoid of reality; the path of words and letters is severed, and they are inconceivable."
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta said:
"It is not that it is not real; it exists in accordance with reality.
The Buddha said:
"Non-existence does not abide in non-existence, and existence does not abide in existence; it is neither non-existent nor existent.
As for the dharma that is not existent, it does not abide in non-existence;
as for the characteristic that is not non-existent, it does not abide in existence. The principle cannot be expressed through the categories of existence and non-existence."
Bodhisattva!
The characteristics of names and meanings are inconceivable. Why is this?
"The name that is nameless is not without a name;
the meaning that is meaningless is not without meaning.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta said:
"Such names and meanings are the true suchness (*tathatā*).
The suchness of the Tathāgata does not abide in suchness; suchness has no characteristic of suchness.
Because its characteristics are without suchness, it is not non-Tathāgata."
"The mental characteristics of sentient beings are themselves the Tathāgata;
the mind of sentient beings should have no separate object.
The Buddha said:
"It is so. The minds of sentient beings truly have no separate objects. Why is this?
Because the mind is fundamentally pure and, in principle, devoid of defilement, it is called the "Three Realms" (tridhātu) due to its being stained by dust-like afflictions.
The mind within these Three Realms is termed the "distinctive object" (viṣayaviśeṣa).
"These objects are illusory, produced through the transformations of the mind;
if the mind were without delusion, there would be no separate objects.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva said:
"If the mind is pure, no objects arise.
When this mind is pure, there should be no triple world.
The Buddha said:
"Thus it is, O Bodhisattva!
The mind does not give rise to objects, and objects do not give rise to the mind."
Why is this? All objects perceived are merely the mind that perceives; if the mind does not manifest through illusory transformation, there would be nothing perceived.
O Bodhisattva!

Within, there are no sentient beings; the three natures are empty and quiescent. Thus, there is neither one's own assembly nor another's assembly, and even regarding the two entrances, no mind arises.
When one attains such benefit, there is no longer the triple world.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva asked:
“How is it that the two entrances do not arise in the mind?”
“The mind is fundamentally unarisen; how could there be entry?
The Buddha said, “There are two entries:”
The first is called entry through principle; the second is called entry through practice.

"Entry through principle" means to have deep faith that sentient beings do not differ from true nature, being neither identical nor distinct, and that they are merely obscured by adventitious defilements, which neither come nor go.
Steadfastly abide in contemplative observation and discern the Buddha-nature: it is neither existent nor non-existent, without self and without other, for the ordinary and the sage are not two.
When the adamantine ground of the mind is firmly established and immovable—tranquil, unconditioned, and free from discrimination—this is called "entry through principle."

"One who enters into practice does not lean toward or depend upon anything; their reflection is free from fluctuation. In all circumstances, they maintain tranquil mindfulness without seeking, remaining unmoved by the winds like the great earth."
Having relinquished the mind of self, one delivers sentient beings; being without birth and without marks, there is neither grasping nor abandoning.
"Bodhisattva! The mind has no entering or exiting; because there is no mind that enters or exits, and because of this non-entering, it is called 'entering.'"
Bodhisattva!
Entering the Dharma in this way, the characteristics of dharmas are not empty.
Since the dharmas are not empty, they are not discarded in vain.
"Why is this? Because that which is not non-existent is replete with merit; it is neither mind nor reflection, but is inherently pure by its very nature.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
"What is meant by 'neither mind nor reflection, but naturally pure'? The Buddha said:

"The dharma of emptiness-as-such is not a dharma of mental consciousness; it is not a dharma possessed by the afflictions of the mind; it is not a dharma of the characteristic of emptiness, nor a dharma of the characteristic of form; it is not a conditioned dharma dissociated from the mind, nor an unconditioned dharma associated with the mind; it is not a manifested reflection, nor something displayed; it is not self-nature, nor differentiation; it is not name, nor characteristic, nor meaning."
Why is this? Because meaning has no suchness (*tathatā*).
There is neither a dharma of suchness nor an absence of suchness; there is neither existence nor suchness, nor is it the case that it is not the absence of suchness.
Why is this? The principle of the faculties (indriya) is neither principle nor faculty; it is free from all disputes, and its characteristics are not perceived.
O Bodhisattva!
"Such pure dharmas are not produced by that which produces production, nor extinguished by that which extinguishes extinction.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta said, "Inconceivable!"

Such is the characteristic of phenomena: they do not form a composite, nor do they exist as solitary entities; they are neither bound nor fettered, neither gathered nor dispersed; they are neither born nor extinguished, and they possess no characteristics of coming, going, or abiding.
"It is inconceivable! The Buddha said, "So it is."
Inconceivable! The inconceivable mind is such that the mind itself is also like this. Why is this?
Just as the mind is not different from suchness, for the mind is fundamentally suchness;
so too, the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither identical nor different.
The nature of sentient beings is fundamentally without arising or ceasing; the nature of arising and ceasing is itself fundamentally nirvana.
The nature and characteristics are fundamentally suchness; because suchness is without movement, the characteristics of all phenomena do not arise from conditions.
Since the nature of arising characteristics is suchness, and suchness is unmoving, the nature and characteristics of causes and conditions are fundamentally empty and non-existent.
Conditions and conditions themselves are empty; there is no arising through conditions. All dharmas of conditioning are but the deluded mind’s false perceptions.
Manifestation is fundamentally unarisen because conditions are fundamentally non-existent; the mind accords with the principle of dharmas, its own essence being empty and void.
Just as that King of Space originally has no dwelling place, yet the minds of ordinary beings falsely discriminate and perceive it;
so too, the mark of suchness is fundamentally neither existent nor non-existent, while the marks of existence and non-existence are seen only as the mind and consciousness.
“Bodhisattva!
Such mental phenomena do not lack intrinsic nature, yet their intrinsic nature does not exist; they are neither existent nor non-existent.
Bodhisattva!”
It is neither non-existence nor the markless; it is not a ground accessible through verbal expression. Why is this?
The dharma of True Suchness (tathatā) is vast and empty, devoid of marks, and is not within the reach of the two vehicles.
"The realm of empty space cannot be measured from within or without; only those who practice the six modes of conduct can know it.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva asked:
"What are these six modes of conduct?"
“I pray that you will explain this for me. The Buddha said:

“The first is the practice of the ten faiths; the second is the practice of the ten abidings; the third is the practice of the ten deeds; the fourth is the practice of the ten dedications; the fifth is the practice of the ten stages; and the sixth is the practice of equal enlightenment.”
"A practitioner who acts in this way is indeed able to know it.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva said:
"The realization of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) is free from coming or going."
“What kind of dharma allows the mind to enter the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)?
The Buddha said:
“As for the dharma of the limit of reality, that dharma has no limit. With a mind that is itself limitless, one enters the limit of reality.”
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta said:
"The mind of boundless wisdom—its wisdom has no limit;
with a limitless mind, one attains mastery over the mind."
With sovereign wisdom, one attains entry into the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
As for those ordinary beings and sentient beings of weak mind whose hearts are frequently gasping,
by what dharma can they be governed so that they may attain a firm mind and enter the limit of reality?
The Buddha said: “Bodhisattva!

As for that panting of the mind, it is due to the inner and outer *anuśayas* (proclivities). Following these proclivities, they flow and pour forth; from these drops a sea is formed. When great winds stir the waves, the great dragons are terrified. Because the mind is terrified, it causes much panting.”
O Bodhisattva!
Cause those sentient beings to abide in the three, guard the one, and enter the Tathāgata-dhyāna.
By means of this meditative concentration, their minds will be free from agitation.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta asked:
"What is meant by 'preserving the three and guarding the one' to enter the Tathāgata-dhyāna?
The Buddha said:
"To preserve the three" means to preserve the three gates of liberation.
"To guard the one" means to guard the suchness of the single mind.
To enter the Tathāgata-dhyāna is to contemplate the purity of the mind according to principle; entering such a ground of mind is to enter the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta said:
"What is the nature of the three gates of liberation?
From what dharma does the contemplation of principle samādhi enter?"
The Buddha said:
"The three liberations are:
liberation through space, liberation through the vajra, and liberation through prajñā."
"In the contemplation of principle, the mind is pure according to that principle; there is no 'non-mind' to be found.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva asked:
"How does it preserve its function?"
"How should one contemplate this?
The Buddha said,
"When the mind and phenomena are non-dual, this is called 'preserving function'."
Internal practice and external practice are non-dual in their coming and going; one does not dwell in a single characteristic.
With a mind free from gain and loss, neither fixed nor unfixed, the pure mind flows in—this is called contemplation.
O Bodhisattva!
Such a person does not abide in dualistic characteristics.
Although they do not leave the household life, they do not dwell in the household life either.

Although they do not wear the dharma robes, do not fully observe the prātimokṣa precepts, and do not participate in the poṣadha ceremony, they are able to attain the fruits of sainthood through the unconditioned self-mastery of their own minds.
"Not abiding in the two vehicles, one enters the path of the bodhisattvas; later, one shall fulfill the stages and attain the Bodhi of Buddhahood.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta said, "Inconceivable!"
Such a person is neither one who has left the household life nor one who has not left it.
Why is this? Because they have entered the abode of nirvana, donned the robe of the Tathāgata, and sat upon the seat of enlightenment; such a person—even if a śramaṇa—should be honored and supported.
The Buddha said: "It is so. Why is this?
Entering the abode of nirvāṇa, the mind transcends the triple world;
donning the robe of the Tathāgata, one enters the realm of the emptiness of dharmas;
sitting upon the seat of bodhi, one ascends to the single stage of perfect enlightenment.
"The minds of such people transcend the two selves; how much more so should they respect and support śramaṇas?
Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva said:
"Just as that single ground and the ocean of space are not seen by those of the Two Vehicles."
The Buddha said: "It is so.
Those persons of the two vehicles are attached to the savoring of samādhi."

Having attained the body of samādhi within that single ground of the ocean of emptiness, one remains in a state of stupor like one afflicted by alcohol, unable to awaken; even after the passage of many kalpas, one still does not regain consciousness, and only when the "alcohol" has dissipated does one finally awaken to cultivate this practice, subsequently attaining the Buddha-body.

As for that person, having abandoned the icchantika state, they immediately enter the six practices; within the stage of practice, with a single thought of pure mind, they possess the definitive and clear wisdom-power of the vajra, attain the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika), and deliver sentient beings with inexhaustible compassion.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta said,
"Such a person ought not to uphold the precepts, nor should they hold any reverence for those śramaṇas.
The Buddha said:
"To preach the precepts for the sake of others is due to unwholesome pride and the surging of waves.

Just as in that ground of mind, where the ocean of the eight consciousnesses is clear and the flow of the ninth consciousness is pure, the wind cannot move it and no waves arise; so too, the nature of the precepts is equal to emptiness, and those who cling to them are deluded."

Like that person, through the non-arising of the seven and six [categories of phenomena] and the cessation of all conditioned accumulations, they give rise to bodhicitta without departing from the three Buddhas. Within the three signless states, they enter the profound with a compliant mind; they deeply revere the Triple Gem and do not lose their dignified deportment, maintaining sincere respect for those śramaṇas.
“O Bodhisattva!
That benevolent one does not abide in the conditioned or unconditioned dharmas of the world; he enters the three concentrations on emptiness and extinguishes the three states of existence.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Mahābala.

"That benevolent one has resolved upon bodhicitta in the presence of such Buddhas as the Buddha of Perfectly Fulfilled Fruits, the Tathāgatagarbha Buddha, and the Buddha of Physical Form; he has entered the three clusters of precepts;
he does not dwell in their characteristics and extinguishes the mind of the triple world;
he does not abide in the state of quiescence nor abandon the assembly of the worthy, entering the inconceivable ground of non-restraint."
At that time, Śāriputra rose from his seat, stepped forward, and spoke these verses:
“Possessing the ocean of *prajñā*, you do not dwell in the city of *nirvāṇa*;
like that wondrous lotus flower, it does not grow upon the high plateau.”
Throughout immeasurable kalpas, the Buddhas do not abandon their afflictions;
only after delivering the world do they attain [enlightenment], like a lotus emerging from the mud.
Just as those six stages of practice are cultivated by Bodhisattvas;
Just as those three empty villages are the true path to bodhi,
so do I now abide in non-abiding, as the Buddha has taught:
coming and returning again, one emerges only after reaching full perfection.
"Furthermore, I shall cause all sentient beings to be as I am—without duality;
those who come before and those who come after, I shall cause them all to attain perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"Inconceivable! You shall hereafter attain the Way of Bodhi, and immeasurable sentient beings shall transcend the ocean of suffering of birth and death.
At that time, the great assembly all awakened to Bodhi, and the lesser assemblies entered the ocean of the five voids.
Chapter Six: On the Emptiness of True Nature. *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra*, Chapter Six: On the Emptiness of True Nature. At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Venerable One!..."
The cultivation of the bodhisattva path is devoid of names and characteristics, and the threefold precepts have no formal ritual.
How, then, can one embrace and teach them for the sake of sentient beings?
I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will explain this for me.
The Buddha said:
"Good son! Listen attentively now, and I shall proclaim it for you."
"Good son! Wholesome and unwholesome dharmas are produced through transformation from the mind.
All objective realms are conceptualizations of mental discourse; if one restrains them in a single place, all conditions will be severed and extinguished."
Why is this? Good son! When the single source does not arise, the three functions have nothing to bestow.
"Abiding in accordance with reality, the gates to the six realms are closed;
the four conditions are harmonious, and the three precepts are fully possessed. Śāriputra said:
“What are the four conditions that are compliant, whereby the three precepts are fully possessed?
The Buddha said:
“The four conditions are:”
First is the condition of exercising the power of analytical cessation to grasp [the object], which is the precept of restraining oneself;
second is the condition arising from the accumulation of the power of the fundamentally beneficial and pure faculties, which is the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas;
third is the condition of the power of fundamental wisdom and great compassion, which is the precept of benefiting sentient beings.
The fourth refers to the condition of the power of the wisdom that universally awakens to all things, which accords with abiding in suchness;
these are called the four conditions. Good son!

Thus, by the power of conditions consisting of the four great elements, there is no abiding in the characteristics of things, yet it is not without functional activity; apart from these, they cannot be sought. Good son!
"In this way, a single matter universally encompasses the six practices; this is the Buddha’s bodhi, the ocean of sarvajñā (all-knowledge). Śāriputra said:
"Not abiding in the characteristics of phenomena, yet not being without effort—this is the true emptiness of dharmas, which is eternal, blissful, self, and pure."
Transcending the two types of self and attaining Great Parinirvāṇa, with a mind that is unattached—this is the contemplation of great power.
Within this awakening of contemplation, one should fully possess the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
The Buddha said: "It is so;
one is endowed with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. Why is this?"

The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, and so forth—these many names share a single meaning; they are neither identical nor different.
Because they are merely names and numbers, there is only naming and only characters; phenomena (dharma) cannot be apprehended.
This non-apprehension of phenomena is a single meaning without words; this wordless characteristic and meaning is true emptiness (śūnyatā).
The meaning of emptiness is suchness as it truly is; the principle of suchness encompasses all phenomena.
Noble son! Those who abide in the principle of suchness transcend the ocean of the three sufferings.
Śāriputra said: "All phenomena are entirely composed of words and letters;
the nature of words and letters is not the ultimate meaning."
"The meaning of reality as it truly is cannot be expressed in words.
How, then, does the Tathāgata now preach the Dharma?
The Buddha said:
“I preach the Dharma because you sentient beings speak while remaining within birth.
That which cannot be spoken is spoken; therefore, I speak it.
What I have spoken consists of the meaning, not the words.”
When sentient beings speak, it is words and phrases, not the meaning.
That which is not the meaning is entirely empty and non-existent.
As for these words of emptiness and non-existence, there is no speaking regarding the meaning.
That which does not accord with the meaning is all false speech.
As for speech that accords with the meaning: reality is empty yet not empty; emptiness is real yet not real. It is free from these two characteristics, and there is no middle state between them.
The Dharma that is not "middle" is free from the three marks and no location can be perceived.

As it truly is, so it is spoken: as for suchness, there is no non-existence; in non-existence, there is no existence. As for such non-existence, there is no existence within existence; as for such existence and non-existence, they do not abide.

"Because it is said that [the teaching] does not exist within the teaching, it does not abide in suchness; suchness does not possess suchness, yet there is no absence of suchness in its teaching. Śāriputra said:
"All sentient beings [arise] from icchantika."
"In what stage does the mind of an icchantika abide so as to reach the Tathāgata and the true reality (tathatā) of the Tathāgata?
The Buddha said:
"From the mind of an icchantic up to the Tathāgata, the true reality of the Tathāgata abides in five successive stages."
First is the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*).

One believes that the seed of *tathatā* within this body is obscured by delusion; thus, one abandons the deluded mind so that the pure mind becomes clear and white, and understands that all objective realms are merely mental verbal discriminations.
Second is the stage of reflection (*manasikāra*).

As for reflection: one contemplates that all objects are merely mental verbalizations (*manojalpa*), and that these mental verbalizations and conceptual discriminations manifest according to the mind. One realizes that the perceived objects are not one's own fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*); and that this fundamental consciousness is neither a phenomenon (*dharma*) nor an object-meaning (*artha*), and is neither the grasped (*grāhya*) nor the grasper (*grāhaka*).
Third is the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāvasthā*).

As for "cultivation," it refers to that which constantly arises and is capable of arising; at the very moment of its arising, it is preceded by the guidance of wisdom, which dispels all obstacles and difficulties, leading to liberation from the entanglements of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
Fourth is the stage of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*). As for the practitioner:

having departed from the stages of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra-bhūmi*), the mind is free from grasping or rejecting; the faculties are utterly pure and sharp; the mind is immovable and tranquil; it is determined upon the true nature (*dharmatā*), the Great Parinirvāṇa, which is solely the greatness of essential emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
Fifth is the relinquishing of the station (*sthāna*).

"Relinquishing" means not dwelling in the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), yet the flow of correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) continues; great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is the aspect of suchness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*), yet the aspect does not dwell in suchness. One does not realize *samyaksaṃbodhi* with a hollow mind, for the mind has no boundaries and no location is perceived; this is to reach Tathāgatahood.
"Good son! The five stages and one awakening enter from the fundamental benefit; if one transforms sentient beings, one does so from their fundamental station. Śāriputra said:
"How does one proceed from its original locus?
The Buddha said:
"Originally there is no origin; it abides in non-abiding. Entering the reality of the realm of emptiness, one gives rise to the bodhicitta and thereby fulfills the attainment of the holy path."
Why is this? Good son!
It is like a hand grasping space: it neither obtains it nor does it not obtain it.
Śāriputra said: "As Your Honor has explained, that which precedes all activities and is grasped through its fundamental benefit is the mindfulness of cessation; this cessation is suchness."
It upholds all virtues and encompasses all phenomena, being perfectly integrated and non-dual.
It is inconceivable!
You should know that this Dharma is the Mahāprajñāpāramitā; it is the great divine mantra, the great illuminating mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, and the mantra equal to the unequaled.
The Buddha said: “So it is, so it is.
The fire of the wisdom of the emptiness of nature burns away all fetters within the emptiness of true suchness.”

Equal and perfectly equal, the three stages of Equal Enlightenment and the three bodies of Wondrous Enlightenment are brilliantly clear and pure within the nine consciousnesses, free from all shadows. Good son!
This Dharma is neither cause nor condition, for wisdom functions autonomously;
it is neither moving nor still, for its nature is empty;
its meaning is neither existence nor non-existence, for the characteristic of emptiness itself is empty.
“Good son! If one transforms sentient beings, causing them to contemplate and enter into this meaning—those who enter into this meaning see the Tathāgata. Śāriputra said:
“The Tathāgata’s contemplation of the meaning does not abide in any of the streams; he should transcend the four dhyānas and go beyond the Peak of Existence.
The Buddha said, “It is so.”
Why is this? All dharmas are merely names and numbers; the four dhyānas are likewise so.

One who perceives the Tathāgata sees that the Tathāgata’s mind is sovereign, ever abiding in the state of cessation, neither emerging nor entering, because it is equal in regard to both the internal and the external.
Good son! Just as those various meditative absorptions are all for the sake of the concentration on the emptiness of perception, this Suchness is not, moreover, any of those. Why is this?

To contemplate suchness by means of suchness, one truly does not see any contemplation; the characteristics of suchness and all other characteristics have already ceased. This cessation is the meaning of suchness.
To conceive of meditative concentration as suchness is movement, not true dhyāna.

Why is this? Because the nature of dhyāna is free from all movement; it is neither defilement nor that which is defiled, neither the dharma nor its reflection, and is free from all discrimination, for it is the meaning of primordial benefit.
"Good son! Contemplating concentration in this manner is what is called dhyāna. Śāriputra said:
“Inconceivable! The Tathāgata always transforms sentient beings through that which is according to reality.
Such true meaning, with its manifold expressions and extensive significance, can be cultivated only by those of sharp faculties; for those of dull faculties, it is difficult to apply their minds.”
"What skillful means can be used to enable those of dull faculties to enter this Truth?
The Buddha said,
"If one causes those of dull faculties to receive and uphold even a single four-line verse, they will immediately enter the True Reality."
"All the Buddha-dharmas are encompassed within a single four-line verse.
Śāriputra asked: "What is this four-line verse?"
"I pray that you will explain this for me. Thereupon, the Venerable One spoke in verse:
"The meaning of that which is produced by causes and conditions— this meaning is cessation, not arising."
"The meaning of extinguishing all arising and ceasing—this meaning gives rise [to wisdom], it does not cease.

At that time, the great assembly, having heard this verse, were all filled with great joy; they all attained the ocean of wisdom of the emptiness of nature (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*), which extinguishes arising and ceasing while giving rise to [the realization of] non-arising.
7. The Tathāgata-garbha Section of the Vajrasamādhi Sūtra: The Tathāgata-garbha Section, Seventh. At that time, the Elder Brahmacārin arose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Venerable One!
The meaning of arising is non-extinction, and the meaning of extinction is non-arising; suchness in this sense is precisely the Bodhi of the Buddha.
The nature of Bodhi is non-discriminative, yet non-discriminative wisdom discerns without end.
The characteristic of infinity is the mere cessation of conceptual discrimination; such a characteristic of meaning is inconceivable, and within the inconceivable, there is no discrimination.
Venerable One!
"All dharmas are infinite and boundless in number; yet the nature of the single reality within these boundless characteristics abides in a single essence.
What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha said:
“Householder! It is inconceivable!
I have taught all dharmas for the sake of those who are deluded and as a skillful means to guide them; yet the characteristics of all dharmas are the wisdom of the single true meaning.”

Why is this? It is like a marketplace that has four great gates; though all enter through these four gates, they all return to the same marketplace, just as the multitude enters according to their own inclinations.
The various flavors of the Dharma are likewise so.
The householder Brahmācārin said,
"If the Dharma is thus, I abide in a single flavor (ekarasa), which should encompass all flavors.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is. Why is this? Because the single flavor of the true meaning is like a great ocean; there are no streams that do not enter it."
"O Householder!
The flavor of all dharmas is like those various streams; though their names and numbers differ, their water is no different.
If one dwells in the great ocean, one encompasses all streams; if one dwells in the single flavor, one subsumes all flavors."
The householder Brahmachari said:
"All dharmas are of one flavor.
How can there be differences in the wisdom of the paths of the three vehicles?"
The Buddha said, “Householder!

It is like the Yangtze, the Yellow River, the Huai, and the ocean. Because they differ in size, because they vary in depth, and because their names and designations are distinct, water within the Yangtze is called ‘Yangtze water,’ water within the Huai is called ‘Huai water,’ water within the Yellow River is called ‘Yellow River water,’ yet when all are together in the ocean, they are called only ‘ocean water.’”
The Dharma is also like this: both reside within True Suchness (tathatā), and are designated solely as the Buddha-way.
Householder!
By abiding in the single Buddha-way, one immediately penetrates the three practices.
The householder Brahmācārin asked,
"What are the three types of conduct?
The Buddha said:
"First, practice according to phenomena; second, practice according to consciousness; third, practice according to suchness.
Householder!
These three practices encompass all gateways; there is no gateway among all dharmas that does not enter through them."
One who enters by this practice does not give rise to the mark of emptiness;
one who enters in this manner may be said to enter the Tathāgatagarbha,
for entering the Tathāgatagarbha consists in neither entering nor non-entering.
The Elder Brahmacharin said: "Inconceivable!
Entering the Tathāgatagarbha is like a sprout ripening into fruit; there is no point of entry."
"If their fundamental roots are sharp and powerful, and they achieve benefit by attaining the source, and having attained the source, the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi)—
how great would their wisdom be? The Buddha said, "Their wisdom would be inexhaustible."
To speak briefly, there are four kinds of wisdom. What are these four? First is fixed wisdom, which is said to accord with suchness;

second is unfixed wisdom, which is said to employ skillful means to eliminate afflictions; third is nirvana wisdom, which is said to eliminate the boundary of conceptual awakening; and fourth is ultimate wisdom, which is said to enter reality and fully realize the Buddha-way.
"Elder! These four great functions have been taught by the Buddhas of the past; they are a great bridge and a great ford.
If you would transform sentient beings, you should employ this wisdom."
“Householder! This great application has three further great matters.

First, within the three samādhis, internal and external states do not mutually supplant one another. Second, regarding the categories of the Great Meaning, one selects cessation according to the Path. Third, within the concentration of wisdom as it truly is, one benefits both self and others through compassion.”
These three matters bring about the accomplishment of Bodhi;
if one does not practice these matters, one will be unable to flow into that ocean of the four wisdoms and will allow the great Māras to find their opportunity.
"Elders! You and this great assembly should constantly practice this until you attain Buddhahood, never allowing it to be lost for even a moment.
The Elder Brahmacharin said:
“What are the three samādhis?
The Buddha said:
“The three samādhis are the so-called emptiness samādhi, the signless samādhi, and the wishless samādhi; such are the samādhis.”
The householder Brahmācārin asked,
"What is the section on the Great Meaning?
The Buddha said:

"Great" refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); "meaning" refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*); and "classification" refers to the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
This is what is meant by "the classification of the great meaning. The Elder Brahmacarin said: "Inconceivable!"
Such wisdom and its activities benefit both oneself and others, transcend the stages of the three realms, do not abide in nirvana, and enter the path of the bodhisattva.
Such characteristics of phenomena are subject to arising and ceasing because they are based on conceptual discrimination;
if one were free from discrimination, phenomena would not cease.
At that time, the Tathāgata, wishing to proclaim this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Phenomena arise from conceptual construction, And they likewise cease through conceptual construction.
When all phenomena of conceptual construction are extinguished, These phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing."
At that time, having heard these verses being spoken, the householder Brahmācārin was filled with great joy and delight. Desiring to proclaim their meaning, he spoke these verses:
"All phenomena are fundamentally quiescent; Even this quiescence is without arising.
These various phenomena of arising and ceasing— Such phenomena are not non-arising."
That is not shared with this, because it involves the extremes of annihilation and permanence;
this, however, is free from these two and does not abide in oneness either.
If one says that phenomena possess oneness, such a characteristic is like seeing a mass of hairs [in the air].
Like the delusion of water in a mirage, it exists because of various falsehoods;
if one sees that phenomena do not exist, then these phenomena are identical to space.
Like the delusion of a blind man who does not see the sun, to speak of such phenomena is like describing the hair of a tortoise.
Now that I have heard the Buddha’s teaching, I know that dharmas are not found within dualistic views, nor do they abide in a middle; therefore, I take them from non-abiding.
All the dharmas taught by the Tathāgata arise entirely from non-abiding.
From the place of non-abiding, I pay homage here to the Tathāgata.
I revere the marks of the Tathāgata, equal to space and possessing immovable wisdom;
unattached and without location, I revere the body that dwells nowhere.
"In all places, I constantly see all the Tathāgatas;
I only pray that all the Tathāgatas will explain the eternal Dharma for me.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke these words:
“O sons of good family!
Listen attentively; for you all, I shall expound the eternal Dharma.
Sons of good family!

The eternal dharma is not a non-eternal dharma; it is neither speech nor letters, neither truth nor liberation, neither non-existence nor an objective realm, transcending all delusions and the limits of annihilation.

This Dharma is not impermanent; it is free from all views of permanence and annihilation. To clearly perceive consciousness as permanent—this consciousness is eternally quiescent, and even that quiescence is itself quiescent.
"Good son! One who knows that dharmas are quiescent does not seek to quiesce the mind, for the mind is eternally quiescent;
one who has attained quiescence maintains constant true contemplation, knowing that all names and forms are nothing but the deluded mind."
The deluded mind discriminates and discriminates all phenomena; there is nothing else that arises apart from name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

Knowing phenomena to be thus, one does not follow after words and phrases; with every thought focused on the meaning, one does not discriminate a self. Knowing that "self" is a mere provisional designation, one immediately attains quiescence.
"If one attains quiescence, one immediately attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the elder Brahmācārin, having heard these words, spoke in verse:
"Designation, characteristic, and conceptualization—these matters, along with the name of 'dharmas,' constitute the triad."
True Suchness and the Right Sublime Wisdom, along with those that constitute the five [aggregates].
I now know these dharmas, which are bound by the extremes of annihilation and permanence;
they enter the path of arising and ceasing, being subject to annihilation and not to permanence.
The Tathāgata teaches the Dharma of emptiness, Which is far removed from the extremes of annihilation and permanence.
Dependent origination is never non-arising; Because it does not arise, it does not cease.
To grasp dependent origination as being existent Is like picking flowers out of the sky.
It is like taking the daughter of a barren woman, who ultimately cannot be found.
Apart from the grasping of various causes and conditions, it does not cease through anything else.
Reaching the greatness of its own principle, it attains reality by relying on suchness.
Therefore, the dharma of suchness is eternally sovereign and as-it-is;
all myriad phenomena are not transformations produced by consciousness.
Phenomena apart from consciousness are emptiness; thus, it is from the standpoint of emptiness that this is taught.
Having extinguished all phenomena of arising and ceasing, one abides in nirvāṇa.
Yet, being seized by great compassion, one does not abide in the extinction of nirvāṇa;
by transforming the grasped and the grasper, one enters the Tathāgatagarbha.
At that time, when the great assembly heard this teaching, they all attained right livelihood and entered the ocean of the Tathāgata’s *tathāgatagarbha*.

Chapter Eight: The Chapter on Dharanis The Vajrasamādhi Sūtra, Chapter Eight: The Chapter on Dharanis At that time, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva rose from among the assembly, approached the Buddha, joined his palms, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable One!..."
I observe that the minds of this great assembly harbor doubts that have yet to be resolved.

Now that the Tathāgata desires to eliminate these doubts for them, I shall now ask questions on their behalf according to their uncertainties; I pray that the Buddha, out of his compassion, will graciously grant me permission to speak.
The Buddha said, “Bodhisattva-mahāsattva!
That you are able to deliver sentient beings in this manner is inconceivable great compassion.”
"You should ask extensively, and I shall explain it for you.
Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said,
"In what way are all phenomena not dependently originated?"
At that time, the Tathāgata, wishing to proclaim this meaning, spoke these verses:
“If a phenomenon is produced by conditions, That phenomenon could not exist apart from those conditions.”
"How can it be that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is non-existent, yet conditions can give rise to phenomena?
At that time, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said:
"If phenomena are without arising, how can one say that phenomena arise from the mind?"
Thereupon, the Venerable One spoke these verses:
