"These phenomena are born of the mind; These phenomena are that which is grasped and that which grasps.
Like flowers in the sky seen by a drunken eye, Such are these phenomena, yet they are not that."
At that time, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said:
"If the Dharma is thus, then the Dharma is without dependence; as for a Dharma without dependence, the Dharma should be self-existent."
Thereupon the Venerable One spoke these verses:
“The Dharma is fundamentally neither existent nor non-existent; self and other are likewise so.
It has no beginning and no end; its arising and ceasing do not abide.”
At that time, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said:
"The characteristics of all dharmas are themselves primordial nirvāṇa; the same is true for the characteristics of nirvāṇa and emptiness."
"There are no such dharmas; these dharmas are thusness.
The Buddha said:
"There are no such dharmas; these dharmas are thusness."
Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said: “Inconceivable!
Suchness (tathatā) is neither shared nor unshared; whether grasped by the mind or grasped by karma, it is in every way empty and quiescent.”
"The mind and dharmas are both empty and quiescent; neither can be grasped, and they should likewise be extinguished.
Thereupon, the Venerable One spoke these verses:
"All dharmas are empty and quiescent; These dharmas are quiescent, yet not empty."
"When that mind is not empty, / This mind is attained as non-existent.
At that time, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said:
"This dharma is not the three truths; form is empty and mind is also extinguished. When this dharma is fundamentally extinguished, this dharma should be extinction itself."
Thereupon the Venerable One spoke these verses:
“Phenomena originally lack intrinsic nature; They arise from that [conditionality]. In such a place, there is not That which is thus.”
At that time, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said:
"All dharmas are without arising and without cessation.
Why, then, would they not be one?"
Thereupon the Venerable One spoke these verses:
“The abiding place of phenomena has no location; Because their characteristics and enumerations are empty, they do not exist.
The two—name and description—and the phenomenon itself: These constitute the grasper and the grasped.”
At that time, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said:
“The characteristics of all dharmas do not abide on the two shores, nor do they abide in the middle stream;
the mind and consciousness are likewise.”
How do all objects arise from consciousness? If consciousness has the capacity to produce, then this consciousness itself must also arise from something produced.
How can a consciousness that is unarisen produce that which is produced?
Thereupon, the Venerable One spoke these verses:
“The produced and that which produces—these two are the grasper and the grasped.
Both are fundamentally non-existent in themselves; their apprehension is like a flower in the sky or a magical illusion.”
When consciousness arises, the object has not yet arisen;
when the object arises, consciousness has already ceased.
Thus, they are fundamentally non-existent together, nor is there existence or non-existence.
"If there is no arising, consciousness also does not exist; how then can objects arise from existence?
At that time, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said:
"The nature of phenomena is thus: both internal and external are empty."
"The two categories of object and wisdom are originally quiescent and extinguished.
The true mark of ultimate emptiness spoken of by the Tathāgata—such a dharma is not a collection.
The Buddha said:

"It is so. The Dharma as it truly is is formless, non-abiding, neither that which is accumulated nor that which accumulates, neither meaning nor great; it is the single root of beneficial dharmas, a profound mass of merit."
Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said: “Inconceivable!

This inconceivable assembly is such that the seven and five do not arise; the eight and six are quiescent; the nine marks are empty and non-existent; where there is existence, there is no existence; where there is non-existence, there is no non-existence.”
As the Venerable One has taught, all dharmas are empty; yet one enters emptiness without ceasing activity, and does not lose the continuity of karma.
Being without self or what belongs to a self, the views of a body as subject and object, and all internal and external fetters, are entirely stilled; therefore, even aspiration ceases.
"Such is the contemplation of principle: wisdom and concentration are true suchness.
The Venerable One often says that the reality of the dharma of emptiness is indeed a potent medicine.
The Buddha said:
"It is so. Why is this? Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is empty."
Emptiness is unborn, and the mind is eternally unborn;
emptiness is unceasing, and the mind is eternally unceasing;
emptiness is non-abiding, and the mind likewise does not abide.
Emptiness is unconditioned, and the mind is likewise unconditioned.
Emptiness has no coming or going; it is free from all gain and loss, and the elements, aggregates, and sense bases are all likewise non-existent.
The mind’s lack of attachment is also just like this.
"O Bodhisattva!
I speak of the dharma of emptiness: like the water in a mirage, one knows it is not non-existent, yet it arises from the nature of fire. One who contemplates in this way possesses wisdom."
The Buddha said: “It is so. Why is this?

This person’s true contemplation is to contemplate the single state of quiescence, wherein both characteristics and non-characteristics are equalized through emptiness; because they grasp emptiness to cultivate emptiness, they do not fail to see the Buddha.
Because they see the Buddha, they do not follow the three currents within the Mahāyāna.
The three paths of liberation are of one essence and lack intrinsic nature; because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty;
because they are empty, they are signless;
because they are signless, they are wishless.
Because there is no volitional action, there is no seeking;
because there is no seeking, there is no wishing;
because there is no wishing, one thereby understands karma, and thus the mind must be purified.
Because the mind is pure, one is able to see the Buddha;
because one sees the Buddha, one shall be born in the Pure Land.
O Bodhisattva!
Thereupon, through diligent cultivation of the profound Dharma and the three transformations, his wisdom and concentration were perfected, and he immediately transcended the three realms.
Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said:
"That which the Tathāgata has spoken of as neither arising nor ceasing is itself impermanence."

This cessation is the cessation of arising and ceasing. Once arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescent extinction is the eternal. Because it is eternal, it is uninterrupted; this is the dharma of non-interruption.
Transcending all three realms, whether phenomena are mobile or immobile, one should regard conditioned phenomena as avoiding a pit of fire.
"By relying on what dharma does one reproach oneself and enter that single gate?
The Buddha said, "Bodhisattva!"
"One should rebuke one's mind regarding three great matters and enter into practice through the three great truths.
Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva asked:
"What are the three matters by which one rebukes the mind?"
"How does one enter the single practice through the three truths?
The Buddha said,
"The three great matters are:"
The first refers to the cause, the second to the fruit, and the third to consciousness.
These three things have been empty and non-existent from the very beginning; they are neither the self nor a true self.
Why, then, do you give rise to attachment and defilement toward them?
Contemplating these three matters, one sees how one is bound by fetters and adrift in the ocean of suffering; for this reason, one should constantly reproach oneself.
"The three great truths are:

first, the path of Bodhi is the truth of equality, not the truth of inequality; second, the attainment of truth through the right wisdom of Great Enlightenment, not the attainment of truth through false wisdom; third, the entry into truth through the non-dual practice of wisdom and concentration, not the entry into truth through mixed practices."
By practicing the path to Buddhahood through these three truths, there is no one who will not attain perfect enlightenment within this Dharma.
Having attained the wisdom of perfect enlightenment, they flow with great and ultimate compassion; benefiting both themselves and others, they realize the Bodhi of a Buddha.
Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said:
"Venerable One!
Such a dharma is without causes and conditions."
"If there were no dharmas without conditions, causes would not arise.
How, then, does one enter the Tathāgata through the dharma of immovability?
At that time, the Tathāgata, wishing to proclaim this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The characteristics of all phenomena are empty by nature and immovable;
these phenomena do not arise at this time, nor do they arise at any other time.
There is no distinct time for phenomena, nor do they arise at a distinct time."
Dharmas have neither movement nor stillness; because their nature is empty, they are quiescent.
When their nature is empty and quiescent, this dharma and this time manifest;
because they are free from marks, they abide in stillness, and because they abide in stillness, they do not engage with conditions.
These are the phenomena of dependent origination; these phenomena do not arise through conditions.
Since there is no arising or ceasing from causes and conditions, the nature of arising and ceasing is empty and quiescent.
The capacity for conditions constitutes the object of cognition; this conditionality is fundamentally dependent origination.
Therefore, phenomena do not arise from conditions, and the non-arising of conditions is likewise so.
Phenomena produced by causes and conditions—these very phenomena are themselves the causes and conditions;
that which has the characteristic of arising and ceasing through causes and conditions is, in itself, without arising or ceasing.
That which accords with the true nature of reality Is fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing;
Yet at this very time, all phenomena Spontaneously undergo arising and ceasing.
Therefore, the ultimate purity of the source Is fundamentally not produced by the power of manifold conditions.
"Immediately upon reaching that subsequent attainment, one attains what was previously attained.

At that time, when the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha heard what the Buddha had said, his mind felt great joy; and as none among the assembly harbored any doubt, he, knowing the thoughts of the multitude, spoke this verse:
"I knew the doubts in the minds of the assembly, And for that reason I asked with such earnest persistence."
The Tathāgata’s great kindness and compassion distinguish all things without exception.
These two assemblies have all attained clear understanding;
now, from this state of clarity, I universally transform all sentient beings.
"The Great Compassion of the Tathāgata does not abandon his original vow;
therefore, he abides within the afflictions on the ground of the only son.
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the assembly, saying:
"This Bodhisattva is inconceivable; he constantly uproots the suffering of sentient beings through great compassion.

If there are sentient beings who uphold this sutra-dharma or uphold the name of this Bodhisattva, they shall not fall into the evil realms, and all obstacles and difficulties will be entirely extinguished."

If there are sentient beings who, free from all other distracting thoughts, single-mindedly keep this sutra in mind and practice it according to the Dharma, at that time the Bodhisattva will constantly manifest transformation bodies to preach the Dharma for them. He will protect these people, never abandoning them for even a moment, and cause them to swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“You bodhisattvas, when transforming sentient beings, must cause them all to practice such a Mahāyāna of definitive meaning.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and said to him:
“The mass of merit of the Mahāyāna spoken of by the Tathāgata definitively severs the fetters; its benefit of awakening to non-arising is inconceivable.”
What is the name of this Dharma teaching?
How much merit is obtained by receiving and upholding this sutra?
I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will explain this for me.
The Buddha said, “Good son!
The name of this sutra is inconceivable; it is that which all Buddhas of the past have protected and remembered, and it enables one to enter the ocean of the Tathāgata’s omniscience.”
If there are sentient beings who uphold this sutra, they shall have nothing further to seek among all other sutras.
This dharma of the sutra is a dhāraṇī that encompasses all teachings; it gathers the essentials of all sutras and constitutes the fundamental tenet of all these dharmas.
As for the names of this sutra, it is called the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-sūtra*, also called the *Vajrasamādhi*, and also called the *Amitārthasiddhānta*.
If there is anyone who upholds this sutra, they are said to uphold the merits of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas; it is like space, which has no boundaries and is inconceivable.
"What I entrust to you is solely this sutra. Ānanda asked:
"What kind of mental conduct and what kind of person should receive and uphold this sutra?"
The Buddha said:
"Good son! Those who receive, uphold, and recite this sutra will have minds free from gain or loss and will constantly cultivate pure conduct."
If amidst frivolous discourse, one always delights in a tranquil mind;
when entering a village, the mind remains constantly in meditative concentration;
and if dwelling in a household, one does not become attached to the three realms of existence.
This person possesses five kinds of blessings in the present life:

first, they are respected by the multitude; second, their body does not meet with untimely death; third, they are able to debate and refute heterodox arguments; fourth, they delight in delivering sentient beings; and fifth, they are able to enter the noble path.
"Such a person as this shall uphold this sutra. Ānanda said,
"As for such a person, will they deliver all sentient beings and receive offerings?"
The Buddha said:

"Such persons as these can serve as a great field of merit for sentient beings; they constantly practice great wisdom and expound both the provisional and the ultimate—they are the Saṃgha of the Four Reliances."
Regarding all offerings, even those consisting of one's head, eyes, marrow, and brain shall be accepted; how much more so, then, that food and clothing cannot be accepted? Good son!
"Such a person as this is your kinsman and your bridge; how much more so should ordinary people offer them support?
Ānanda asked, "If one receives and upholds this sutra from such a person, and offers support to such a person, how much merit will be gained?"
The Buddha said:

"If there were another person who were to take gold and silver filling an entire city and give it as a gift, it would not be equal to one four-line verse of this sutra being received and upheld from this person."
Making offerings to such a person is inconceivable. Good son!
It causes all sentient beings who uphold this sutra to have their minds constantly in samādhi, never losing their original mind.
"If you lose your original mind, you should immediately repent.
The method of repentance is that which brings coolness. Ānanda said:
"Confessing prior transgressions does not allow them to remain in the past.
The Buddha said, "So it is."
It is just as when a dark room encounters a bright lamp: the darkness is immediately extinguished.
Good son! There is no need to speak of repenting for all previous transgressions, for they are considered to have entered the past by the very act of speaking of them.
Ānanda asked, "What is meant by 'repentance'?
The Buddha said:

"By relying on the teachings of this sutra, one enters into the contemplation of reality; at the moment of entering this contemplation, all transgressions are completely extinguished, one is freed from the evil realms, shall be reborn in a pure land, and will swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, Ānanda, along with all the bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly, were filled with great joy; their minds attained certainty, and they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joyfully putting his teachings into practice.
